# Generalizability of Landmark Temporary MCS Device Trials

**Authors:** Song Li; Claudius Mahr; Rachna Kataria; Van-Khue Ton; Elric Zweck; Manreet K. Kanwar; Shashank S. Sinha; Arthur R. Garan; Jaime Hernandez-Montfort; Jacob Abraham; Daniel Burkhoff; Robert W. Yeh; Jacob Eifer Møller; Holger Thiele; Navin K. Kapur

**Affiliations:** aInstitute for Advanced Cardiac Care, Medical City Healthcare, Dallas, Texas, USA | bBrown University Health, Providence, Rhode Island, USA | cMassachusetts General Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | dDepartment of Cardiology, Pulmonology, and Vascular Medicine Heinrich-Heine-University, Düsseldorf, Germany | eUniversity of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois, USA | fInova Heart and Vascular Institute, Inova Fairfax Campus, Falls Church, Virginia, USA | gBeth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | hBaylor Scott & White Health, Advanced Heart Failure Program Clinic, Temple, Texas, USA | iCenter for Cardiovascular Analytics, Research and Data Science, Providence Heart Institute, Portland, Oregon, USA | jCardiovascular Research Foundation, New York, New York, USA | kOdense University Hospital, Odense, Denmark | lUniversity of Leipzig - Heart Center, Leipzig, Germany | mThe Cardiovascular Center, Tufts Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Landmark randomized controlled trials like DanGer Shock, IABP-SHOCK II, and ECLS-SHOCK guide infarct-related cardiogenic shock (CS) management with temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS), but strict enrollment criteria may limit real-world applicability.

The objective of the study was to evaluate the eligibility overlap of patients from these three key CS trials with the contemporary CS Working Group registry.

In this retrospective analysis, CS patients enrolled between 2020 and 2024 in the CS Working Group registry were assessed. Using trial-specific enrollment criteria (DanGer Shock, IABP-SHOCK II, and ECLS-SHOCK), subsets of patients meeting these criteria were identified. We compared baseline characteristics and usage patterns of tMCS devices among trial-eligible and trial-ineligible patients.

Only a small proportion of registry patients met all the key enrollment criteria: 19.3% (DanGer Shock), 28.4% (IABP-SHOCK II), and 23.6% (ECLS-SHOCK). Hypotension and elevated lactate thresholds were the most restrictive criteria across trials. Trial-eligible patients had more severe CS and end-organ damage than ineligible patients. Actual device use in real-world practice differed markedly from trial assignments; notably, only 20% of DanGer-like patients received Impella CP as their first device.

Patients meeting the landmark CS trial criteria represent a small, high-risk subset of the real-world CS population, highlighting a substantial evidence gap for the majority of CS patients receiving tMCS in clinical practice. Enhancing registry enrollment of specific CS subsets and adopting innovative analytic strategies could bridge gaps between randomized controlled trials findings and real-world applicability.

## Abstract

The management of cardiogenic shock (CS) remains challenging despite significant advances in temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) technology.1,2 Major randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have informed clinical guidelines for the management of patients with infarct-related CS.3, 4, 5 However, the trials’ strict enrollment criteria often put their applicability to broader patient populations encountered in real-world clinical practice into question.

The DanGer Shock trial was a landmark RCT investigating the role of early MCS with the Impella CP in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)-related CS.5 It demonstrated a 13% absolute reduction in 6-month all-cause mortality compared with the standard medical therapy alone, making it the first RCT to show a survival benefit with MCS in CS. However, the trial had highly selective inclusion criteria, enrolling only STEMI-CS patients with hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <100 mm Hg), hypoperfusion (lactate >2.5 mmol/L), and moderate to severe left ventricular (LV) dysfunction. Those with predominant right ventricular failure, normotensive CS, and patients comatose post–out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) were excluded from the trial. These relatively stringent criteria contributed to slow recruitment over a decade and potentially limit the applicability of its findings to a more diverse “real-world” CS population.

The IABP-SHOCK II trial, another pivotal RCT, investigated intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) therapy in CS patients due to STEMI and non-STEMI (NSTEMI).3 Similarly, the ECLS-SHOCK trial evaluated extracorporeal life support (ECLS) in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI)-related CS (STEMI and NSTEMI).4 Although both trials had broader eligibility criteria than DanGer Shock particularly with regard to CS etiology, the extent to which the results of these trials apply to contemporary CS populations remains uncertain.

Given the challenges faced by RCTs in CS—including slow recruitment, stringent eligibility criteria, and resource-intensive protocols—registries have become valuable tools for evaluating real-world outcomes and potentially assessing the treatment effects of MCS devices through observational approaches that seek to emulate trials (so called “target trial emulation").2,6, 7, 8 In addition, formal comparisons of trial populations with large representative registries such as the CS Working Group (CSWG) can more scientifically assess the applicability of trial findings to contemporary practice.

In this study, we aimed to assess the eligibility overlap between the patient populations of the three contemporary CS trials noted previously and the real-world CSWG registry, and to characterize the phenotypic differences between trial-eligible and trial-ineligible patients.

## Methods

### Data source

This retrospective cohort study used data from the international, multicenter CSWG registry. Detailed descriptions of the registry have been previously reported.2 The CSWG registry enrolls consecutive patients presenting with CS (Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions stages B–E) at participating sites, regardless of etiology. Clinical data, including vital signs, laboratory values, and hemodynamic parameters, are recorded at the time of admission to the participating site, and serially throughout the hospitalization (at 6 hours, 12 hours, 18 hours, 24 hours, 48 hours, 72 hours, and finally before discharge). Relevant to this analysis, blood pressure and lactate levels from the time of admission were used. The investigation conforms with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. This study was approved by the Tufts Health Sciences Institutional Review Board, and all sites received local Institutional Review Board approval. Retrospective, deidentified data were used in this study and patient consent was waived.

### Application of trial enrollment criteria

We included all CS patients enrolled in CSWG between 2020 and 2024. To evaluate the eligibility overlap with the DanGer Shock trial, patients with CS due to STEMI were identified and subcategorized based on the four key DanGer Shock enrollment criteria: 1) SBP <100 mm Hg; 2) serum lactate ≥2.5 mmol/L; 3) LV ejection fraction (LVEF) <45%; and 4) exclusion of comatose OHCA patients.5 Patients on vasopressor medications were grouped into the low BP category as was performed in the trial. We excluded patients transferred from outside facilities because their onset of shock state was either not reported or they met the DanGer exclusion criterion of shock duration >24 hours.

Similarly, to evaluate the eligibility overlap with the IABP-SHOCK II trial, we identified all patients with CS due to AMI (AMI-CS) including STEMI and NSTEMI per the enrollment criteria of the trial.3 We then subcategorized the AMI-CS patients using two additional key enrollment criteria: 1) SBP <90 mm Hg or requiring vasopressors; and 2) serum lactate ≥2 mmol/L. As the CSWG registry does not have detailed data to ascertain whether patients had altered mental status, cold/clammy skin, or oliguria on presentation, we used the trial’s lactate cutoff as the sole marker for end-organ hypoperfusion. We also excluded patients transferred from outside facilities because in the CSWG registry, we do not know the precise duration of patient’s outside facility length of stay and many transferred patients would meet an IABP-SHOCK II exclusion criterion of shock onset >12 hours before screening.

Lastly, we applied enrollment criteria reflecting the ECLS-SHOCK trial. The ECLS-SHOCK trial is a trial of AMI-CS patients and had near identical key enrollment criteria as the IABP-SHOCK II trial.4 The only major difference is that the lactate threshold for hypoperfusion was a serum lactate ≥3 mmol/L. Otherwise the same methods were followed as for the IABP-SHOCK II trial.

The number and percentages of patients in the CSWG meeting any and all combinations of the key enrollment criteria were tallied for each of the three included RCTs. In addition, the clinical characteristics and the distribution of initial MCS device choice were compared between “trial-eligible” and “trial-ineligible” patients for each of the three trials.

### Statistical methods

Missing values in the trial eligibility variables were imputed using an iterative imputation approach with random forest estimation (scikit-learn IterativeImputer with RandomForestRegressor). Variables used for the imputation included age, sex, SBP, lactate, LVEF, OHCA status, and ventilator status. Imputation was performed because 25.4% of STEMI-CS patients had missing lactate values and 27.4% had missing LVEF; excluding these patients would systematically underestimate the proportion meeting the trial criteria. SBP was missing in 4.6% of patients. OHCA and ventilator status had negligible missingness (<1%). We additionally performed sensitivity analyses using complete case, best case, and worst case scenarios.

Continuous variables were reported as means and SDs for normal distributions and medians and IQRs for non-normal distributions. Categorical variables were reported as absolute numbers and percentages. Means or medians of continuous variables were compared using independent t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, where appropriate. Categorical variables were compared using chi-square tests. Statistical significance was determined using an alpha of 0.05 for all analyses. All statistical analyses were performed using Python (version 3.13, Python Software Foundation).

## Results

Among 9,681 patients enrolled in the CSWG registry between 2020 and 2024, 4,780 patients presented to a CSWG study site directly without being transferred from another hospital. Of these patients, 481 had CS due to STEMI and 694 had CS due to AMI (STEMI or NSTEMI).

### Patients meeting enrollment criteria for each RCT

Of the 481 patients with CS due to STEMI, 93 patients (19.3%; 95% CI: 16.1%-23.1%) met all the 4 DanGer key enrollment criteria specified previously (Central Illustration). The hypotension criterion (SBP <100 mm Hg or requiring vasopressor support) was the most exclusive of the four, ruling out 54.5% of STEMI-CS patients. The lactate criterion (lactate ≥2.5 mmol/L) was the second most stringent, ruling out 24.9% of STEMI-CS patients.Central IllustrationEligibility Overlap Between Landmark Mechanical Circulatory Support Trials and the Cardiogenic Shock Working Group RegistryAmong 481 STEMI-CS and 694 AMI-CS patients enrolled in the Cardiogenic Shock Working Group (CSWG) registry (2020-2024), 19.3% of STEMI-CS patients met the key DanGer Shock enrollment criteria, 28.4% of AMI-CS patients met the IABP-SHOCK II criteria, and 23.6% met the ECLS-SHOCK criteria. Hypotension was the most restrictive criterion across all three trials. Only 19% to 28% of real-world CS patients had direct trial evidence supporting their mechanical circulatory support management. Of the 694 patients with CS due to AMI, 197 patients (28.4%; 95% CI: 25.2%-31.9%) met both hypotension and hypoperfusion enrollment criteria of the IABP-SHOCK II trial (Central Illustration). The hypotension criterion (SBP <90 mm Hg or requiring vasopressor support) was the more exclusive one, ruling out 68.7% of AMI-CS patients. The lactate criterion (lactate ≥2 mmol/L) was less exclusive, ruling out 15.4% of AMI-CS patients.

Of the 694 patients with CS due to AMI, 164 patients (23.6%; 95% CI: 20.6%-26.9%) met both hypotension and hypoperfusion enrollment criteria of the ECLS-SHOCK trial (Central Illustration). The hypotension criterion (SBP <90 mm Hg or requiring vasopressor support) was the more exclusive one, ruling out 68.7% of AMI-CS patients. The lactate criterion (lactate ≥3 mmol/L) was less exclusive, ruling out 33.4% of AMI-CS patients.

In sensitivity analyses, the proportion of patients meeting all DanGer Shock criteria was 19.5% (complete case, n = 257), 20.2% (best case), and 10.8% (worst case), compared with 19.3% in the primary imputed analysis. Corresponding values for IABP-SHOCK II were 33.1%, 29.7%, and 24.1% (vs 28.4%), and for ECLS-SHOCK were 26.3%, 24.6%, and 19.3% (vs 23.6%). These results confirm that the primary findings are robust to assumptions about missing data.

### Patients meeting enrollment criteria for multiple or no RCTs

Among the 694 AMI-CS patients, 66 (9.5%) met the criteria for all three trials. Seventy-one patients (10.2%) met the criteria for both DanGer Shock and IABP-SHOCK II, and 164 (23.6%) met the criteria for both IABP-SHOCK II and ECLS-SHOCK. All ECLS-SHOCK-eligible patients were also eligible for IABP-SHOCK II, as the only distinguishing criterion is a higher lactate threshold (≥3 vs ≥2 mmol/L). Overall, 475 (68.4%) did not meet the enrollment criteria for any of the three trials.

### Baseline characteristics

Baseline characteristics of patients meeting the key enrollment criteria of each of the three RCTs are shown in Table 1, Table 2, Table 3. These patients are termed “DanGer Shock-like”, “IABP-SHOCK II-like”, or “ECLS-SHOCK-like”, respectively. Patients who did not meet the criteria are also shown in Table 1, Table 2, Table 3 (“ineligible patients”). As expected, trial-eligible patients had more critical values of eligibility-defining variables (SBP, lactate, and LVEF). Beyond these, trial-eligible patients also demonstrated important phenotypic differences in noncriteria variables. Trial-eligible patients tend to have higher creatinine, glucose, white blood cell, alanine aminotransferase, international normalized ratio, and lower platelets and B-type natriuretic peptide, suggestive of a more acute presentation with more severe end-organ dysfunction. Compared to the published trial baseline characteristics, CSWG DanGer Shock-like patients had higher lactate, prior myocardial infarction, hypertension, and diabetes than the RCT, suggestive of more severe shock and more comorbidities. ### Distribution of initial temporary MCS

Among the 93 DanGer Shock-like patients, the distribution of initial MCS device types is depicted in Figure 1. The most commonly used MCS strategies were IABP (31.2%; 95% CI: 22.7%-41.2%), followed by no MCS device (29.0%; 95% CI: 20.8%-38.9%), Impella CP (20.4%; 95% CI: 13.5%-29.7%), and venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) (15.1%; 95% CI: 9.2%-23.7%). Notably, only 19 of the 93 DanGer-like patients received an Impella CP as the initial MCS device. ## Discussion

The current analysis of the CSWG registry provides insights into the real-world applicability of major RCTs evaluating MCS devices. Three main findings were identified: 1) only a small subset of real-world CS patients met the key enrollment criteria of landmark trials including DanGer Shock (19.3%), IABP-SHOCK II (28.4%), and ECLS-SHOCK (23.6%); 2) real-world “trial-eligible” patients represent a very high-risk population compared to “trial-ineligible” patients, with more severe hypotension, hypoperfusion, and end-organ damage; and 3) common MCS devices including IABP, Impella CP, and VA-ECMO continue to have significant usage among real-world patients, whether “trial-eligible” or not.

Among the four key criteria that rendered CSWG registry patients ineligible for DanGer Shock trial, hypotension (SBP <100 mm Hg or vasopressor support) and elevated lactate (≥2.5 mmol/L) were particularly restrictive. These highly selective criteria defined a more homogenous, very high-risk cohort which may have contributed to the effectiveness of the Impella CP in DanGer Shock. This supports the concept that matching the right device to the right patient phenotype is critical for demonstrating benefit in CS, and may serve as a model for future MCS trial design. However, this aspect of trial design presents a clear trade-off which is the resulting low eligibility overlap with a more diverse, real-world CS population. This narrow eligibility overlap means that the majority of patients receiving these devices in clinical practice lack direct trial evidence to guide their management. Specifically, DanGer Shock’s findings are relevant only for the trial-specific STEMI population, which excludes the other ∼80% of STEMI CS patients, let alone other etiologies of CS. The IABP-SHOCK II and ECLS-SHOCK trials enrolled a broader AMI-CS population including both STEMI and NSTEMI. However, their respective enrollment criteria were also quite restrictive resulting in only 28.4% (IABP-SHOCK II) and 23.6% (ECLS-SHOCK) of real-world AMI-CS patients in CSWG being “trial-eligible”.

Furthermore, even among “trial-eligible” real-world patients, important differences exist compared to actual trial participants. Notably, the real-world “trial-eligible” patients in CSWG had significantly higher baseline lactate than reported in patients in the three RCTs (6.4 vs 4.6/4.5 [interventional/control arms] mmol/liter in DanGer Shock, 6.7 vs 3.6/4.7 in IABP-SHOCK II, and 9.4 vs 6.8/6.9 in ECLS-SHOCK, respectively).3, 4, 5 Thus, the characteristics of real-world “trial-eligible” patients do not completely mirror those of the RCT patients and appear to represent an even higher-risk cohort. These discrepancies underscore the ongoing uncertainty regarding the applicability of trial findings, whether positive or negative, to contemporary clinical practice, despite recent updates to the joint societal guideline for the management of patients with acute coronary syndromes.9

The distribution of initial tMCS device utilization in our registry further illustrates the disconnect between controlled trial designs and actual clinical care. The CSWG cohort analyzed here spans a period beginning at least 8 years after the publication of the IABP-SHOCK II trial, aligning with the publication of ECLS-SHOCK, and concluding shortly after the release of the DanGer Shock trial results. Despite the negative trial results for IABP and VA-ECMO, all three tMCS devices tested in these trials continue to be frequently used in both “trial-eligible” and “trial-ineligible” real-world populations. The continued use of IABP and VA-ECMO may reflect appropriate clinician decision-making for patients deemed “nonroutine” or may be influenced by provider experience, resource availability, institutional policies, and reimbursement factors. Whether Impella CP use increases in the post-DanGer trial era with a class 2A recommendation and VA-ECMO and IABP use decreases with a class 3B recommendation remains to be seen.9

The limited eligibility overlap of these RCTs with real-world CS populations and the absence of a clear impact yet on clinical practice illustrate the difficulty of evidence generation and implementation in the CS space. The enrollment criteria of the aforementioned RCTs in a way reflect a strategic dilemma between maximizing the likelihood of finding a beneficial result by selecting a more homogenous, high-risk population vs the broader applicability and clinical impact of such results. However, the risk enrichment based on hypotension and hypoperfusion is relatively 1-dimensional and does not necessarily correlate with maximizing benefit from any particular MCS device. It is conceptually possible that each MCS device has a corresponding “best-fit” patient phenotype that is multidimensional, based on shock etiology, comorbidities, vascular anatomy, hemodynamics, etc. Understanding these phenotypes would greatly aid future trial design.

Given that the goal of evidence-based MCS practice in a large proportion of CS patients is not currently met by the existing RCTs, observational data may help fill important gaps via casual inference techniques including target trial emulation and external control arms.6,10,11 Registries such as the CSWG represent invaluable complements to traditional RCT approaches. However, observational comparisons of MCS devices may be particularly vulnerable to bias due to confounding by indication (ie, treatment selection bias), if data sets do not have sufficiently granular information on shock criteria, shock severity, and hemodynamic profiles.12 The CSWG registry collects detailed information on shock phenotype, hemodynamic status, and medical/device treatment, which, combined with the use of sophisticated statistical methods adhering to the principles of target trial emulation, may offer more valid estimates of treatment effectiveness than previously possible.13 To leverage this approach effectively, however, registries must enroll adequately large, representative patient populations. There remains a critical need to expand enrollment of specific patient subsets within CSWG and other shock registries to facilitate robust trial emulation analyses.

This study has several limitations. First, the vital signs and laboratory values from the CSWG registry used in this analysis were recorded at hospital admission, introducing the possibility that some patients met the hemodynamic criteria transiently but were not classified as trial-eligible based on available data. Second, the registry lacked detailed data on certain trial inclusion/exclusion criteria—including altered mental status, skin perfusion, urine output, and precise timing of shock onset—which could lead to either overestimation or underestimation of trial-eligible populations. Third, variability in institutional policies, resource availability, and clinical decision-making across CSWG sites introduces external factors not fully captured by this analysis. Fourth, the enrollment period of this version of the CSWG registry (2020–mid-2024) largely predates the publication of DanGer Shock results (April 2024), and the observed low utilization of Impella CP among DanGer-eligible patients may not reflect post-trial practice patterns. Fifth, transferred patients (50.6% of total registry) were excluded because the CSWG does not reliably capture the time of shock onset at the transferring facility, but most transferred patients likely are not eligible due to time from onset of CS being a trial criterion. Finally, the CSWG registry, although multicenter and international, may not be fully representative of all CS populations, as participating centers are predominantly academic institutions with MCS capabilities.

In conclusion, although landmark trials such as DanGer Shock, IABP-SHOCK II, and ECLS-SHOCK have provided critically important guidance for clinical practice, their selective enrollment criteria result in low eligibility overlap with broader CS populations, leaving a substantial evidence gap for tMCS device selection in the majority of real-world CS patients. Short of repeating these RCTs, which is expensive and requires many years of trial enrollment, exploring innovative trial designs and incorporating real-world data analytics could provide new insights into treatment effectiveness and inform individualized patient care strategies. Continued investment and strategic development of highly granular CSWG-like registries with temporal resolution across the duration of care are essential to advance CS management and translate research findings into meaningful improvements in real-world patient care.PerspectivesCOMPETENCY IN MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE: Only 19% to 28% of real-world CS patients in a multicenter international registry met the key enrollment criteria of three landmark tMCS trials (DanGer Shock, IABP-SHOCK II, and ECLS-SHOCK), with hypotension thresholds being the most restrictive criterion. Clinicians should recognize that direct RCT evidence currently applies to a minority of CS patients encountered in practice.COMPETENCY IN PATIENT CARE: Trial-eligible patients identified in clinical practice may present with even higher acuity than actual trial participants, as reflected by higher baseline lactate levels. When extrapolating trial results to bedside decisions, clinicians should consider whether an individual patient's phenotype aligns with the population studied in the trial.COMPETENCY IN SYSTEMS-BASED PRACTICE: The marked variation in device utilization patterns across the registry—with many trial-eligible patients receiving no MCS or a device different from the one studied in the trial—underscores the need for institutional protocols that systematically identify candidates who may benefit from evidence-based device selection.TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: The limited eligibility overlap between landmark RCTs and real-world CS populations highlights a substantial evidence gap for the majority of patients. Future research should focus on: 1) pragmatic trial designs with broader enrollment criteria to capture the heterogeneous CS population encountered in clinical practice; 2) observational approaches such as target trial emulation and external control arms using large registries to generate complementary evidence; and 3) phenotype-guided device selection strategies that match specific patient profiles to the MCS device most likely to confer benefit.
